messages.text: ok so I was sketching the pipeline flow. exact match -> trigram fuzzy (>=0.6) -> embedding kNN -> LLM adjudication.
wait, the model is the last resort? that sounds efficient but risky if the embeddings are weird.
yeah, we only call qwen when cheap matching fails. saves latency and cost. the embedding threshold is set to auto-accept >=0.92 though.
that seems high for auto-accept. what happens if it's between 0.6 and 0.92?
llm adjudication picks from top-5 candidates. but here's the kicker: if all candidates are bad, it can propose a new concept.
hold on. user-generated concepts? we just agreed the ontology is static for the hackathon?
it's not user-driven, it's model-driven fallback. but i agree, that's a scope nightmare and privacy risk if we let it mint junk.
definitely need guards. what if someone types "vacation photos"? i don't want that becoming a canonical node.
good catch. let's add a char limit. only propose new concept if the input string is 5+ characters. short stuff gets rejected or forced to existing matches.
5 chars feels arbitrary but okay. "ml" is 2, "deep learning" is 13. so "ml" won't create a new node? that's good.
exactly. also, every model decision gets cached as an alias after the first time. so even if it makes a mistake once, it won't hit the model twice for the same string.
smart. so the cache acts as a safety net too? if i see a bad alias later, i can just edit the db entry and it fixes future looksups?
yes. manual override via the alias table. we'll document that as the "human in the loop" escape hatch for the demo if judges ask.
i like it. i'll update my csv to mark which aliases are manual vs auto-generated so we don't accidentally delete a cached model decision.
perfect. i'll code the pipeline stages in that order then: exact, trigram, embed, adjudicate. will push a branch tomorrow so you can test the thresholds.
